# Including phylogenetic uncertainty - Julia version

Often, we do not have a single phylogeny but a set of phylogenies, e.g., from a Bayesian phylogenetic inference. When using phylogenetic control, we want to marginalize over the phylogenetic uncertainty. Doing this in R + Stan is possible but cumbersome and computationally expensive. Therefore I will explore re-implementations of the R/Stan models in Julia + Turing.jl, and in Python + NumPyro.

Let's start with Julia.

```{julia}
# Create data directory if it doesn't exist
isdir("../data") || mkpath("../data")

# Paths
tgz_url = "https://github.com/rbouckaert/global-language-tree-pipeline/releases/download/v1.0.0/all_trees.tgz"
tgz_file = "../data/all_trees.tgz"
tar_file = "../data/all_trees.tar"
tree_dir = "../data/all_trees/"

# Download and extract
if !isdir(tree_dir)
    Downloads.download(tgz_url, tgz_file)

    # Decompress .tgz to .tar
    open(tgz_file) do f_in
        open(tar_file, "w") do f_out
            write(f_out, transcode(GzipDecompressor, read(f_in)))
        end
    end

    # Extract .tar archive
    Tar.extract(tar_file, tree_dir)
    # Move all files from ../data/all_trees/all_trees to ../data/all_trees
    inner_dir = joinpath(tree_dir, "all_trees")
    if isdir(inner_dir)
        for f in readdir(inner_dir; join=true)
            mv(f, joinpath(tree_dir, basename(f)); force=true)
        end
        rm(inner_dir; force=true, recursive=true)
    end
    # Clean up
    rm(tgz_file)
    rm(tar_file)
end


# Load all Newick trees
tree_files = glob("*.tree", tree_dir)

trees = [parsenewick(read(f, String)) for f in tree_files]

# Optionally strip suffixes
for tree in trees
    for tip in getleaves(tree)
        tip.name = split(tip.name, "_")[1]
    end
end

```

## Vanilla regression

We will use the same model as in the previous notebook, but now we will use Turing.jl to implement it.

The likelihood is implemented as a Turing model like this:

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}
@model function vanilla_regression(; x=d.x)
    N = length(x)
    # Center x
    means_x = mean(x)
    Xc = x .- means_x

    # Priors
    alpha ~ LocationScale(0, 2.5, TDist(3))
    beta ~ Normal(0, 2)

    # Linear predictor
    η = alpha .+ beta .* Xc

    y ~ product_distribution(Bernoulli.(cdf.(Normal(), η)))
    # Likelihood

    loglik := [logpdf(Bernoulli(cdf(Normal(), η[i])), y[i]) for i in 1:N]
    y_rep := [rand(Bernoulli(cdf(Normal(), η[i]))) for i in 1:N]
    return (y=y, loglik=loglik, y_rep=y_rep)
end
```




Let's run the model:

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}

model_vanilla_regression = vanilla_regression() | (y=d.y,)

# Run the model

chain_vanilla_regression = sample(
    model_vanilla_regression,
    NUTS(),
    MCMCThreads(),
    1000,
    4,
    discard_initial=1000,
    progress=true,
)

# Print summary of the chain
describe(chain_vanilla_regression[:, [:alpha, :beta], :])
```

The 95% credible intervals for the parameters are:

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}

hpd(chain_vanilla_regression[:, [:alpha, :beta], :])
```


```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}
# plot the posterior distributions of alpha and beta

ridgelineplot(chain_vanilla_regression, [:beta], title="Posterior distributions of beta")

```

This looks reassuringly similar to the R/Stan model. Now let's plot the prior and posterior predictive distributions.

```{julia}

function predictive_checks_regression(y_rep, y_prior; d=d)
    obs_0 = mean(d.y[d.x.==0])
    obs_1 = mean(d.y[d.x.==1])
    # Define colors
    CBblue = RGB(0.0, 114 / 255, 178 / 255)
    CBvermillion = RGB(213 / 255, 94 / 255, 0.0)

    p0 = density(y_prior[d.x.==0],
        fill=(0, 0.5, CBblue),
        label="Prior",
        title="P(y=1|x=0)"
    )
    density!(p0, y_rep[d.x.==0],
        fill=(0, 0.5, CBvermillion),
        label="Posterior")
    vline!(p0, [obs_0], color=:black, label="", linewidth=2)


    p1 = density(y_prior[d.x.==1],
        fill=(0, 0.5, CBblue),
        label=false,
        title="P(y=1|x=1)"
    )
    density!(p1, y_rep[d.x.==1],
        fill=(0, 0.5, CBvermillion),
        label=false
    )
    vline!(p1, [obs_1], color=:black, label="", linewidth=2)


    link = :both
    plot(p0, p1, layout=(2, 1), link=:x, legend=:topleft)
end

```

Next we sample from the prior and the posterior. In Turing, this is fairly straightforward.

```{julia}
# Prior predictive sampling - sample from prior with missing y
prior_chain = sample(vanilla_regression(), Prior(), 4000)

# Posterior predictive sampling - use the fitted chain

y_rep_names = [v for v in names(prior_chain) if occursin("y_rep", string(v))]

y_prior = mean(Array(prior_chain[:, y_rep_names, :]), dims=1) |> vec

y_rep = mean(Array(chain_vanilla_regression[:, y_rep_names, :]), dims=1) |> vec
```

```{julia}
predictive_checks_regression(y_rep, y_prior)
```

Next we compute the marginal log-likelihood and the LOOIC.

```{julia}
vanilla_regression_target = TuringLogPotential(vanilla_regression() | (y=d.y,))
pt = pigeons(target=vanilla_regression_target, multithreaded=true)
println(stepping_stone(pt))

```



```{julia}

loglik_names = [v for v in names(chain_vanilla_regression) if occursin("loglik", string(v))]

loglik_vanilla = Array(chain_vanilla_regression[:, loglik_names, :])

#| vscode: {languageId: julia}
# Compute LOOIC
loo_vanilla_regression = convert(
    Dict,
    R"
    library(loo)

    ",
);
```

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}

# Alternative: Create a more structured view of LOO results
function format_loo_results(loo_dict)
    # Extract the main metrics
    estimates = DataFrame(
        metric=["LOOIC", "SE of LOOIC", "elpd_loo", "SE of elpd_loo"],
        value=[
            loo_dict["looic"],
            loo_dict["se_looic"],
            loo_dict["elpd_loo"],
            loo_dict["se_p_loo"]
        ]
    )
    return estimates
end

```

```{julia}
# Print LOO results

loo_results_vanilla_regression = format_loo_results(loo_vanilla_regression)
println(loo_results_vanilla_regression)
```

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}

@model function vanilla_correlation(N)
    # Priors
    mu ~ filldist(Normal(0, 2.5), 2)
    rhostar ~ Logistic(0, 1)
    rho := 0.95 * (2 * logistic(rhostar) - 1)  # Keep rho in (-0.95, 0.95)

    # Add small regularization for numerical stability
    eps = 1e-6
    Sigma = [
        1.0+eps rho
        rho 1.0+eps
    ]


    p1 = mvnormcdf(mu, Sigma, [-Inf, -Inf], [0.0, 0.0])[1]
    p2 = mvnormcdf(mu, Sigma, [-Inf, 0.0], [0.0, Inf])[1]
    p3 = mvnormcdf(mu, Sigma, [0.0, -Inf], [Inf, 0.0])[1]
    p4 = mvnormcdf(mu, Sigma, [0.0, 0.0], [Inf, Inf])[1]

    # Ensure all probabilities are positive and sum to something reasonable
    p_raw = [p1, p2, p3, p4]
    p_clean = max.(p_raw, eps)  # Ensure minimum probability
    p_norm = p_clean ./ sum(p_clean)  # Normalize

    xy ~ filldist(Categorical(p_norm), N)

    p_x0 = [p_norm[1], p_norm[2]] / sum([p_norm[1], p_norm[2]])
    p_x1 = [p_norm[3], p_norm[4]] / sum([p_norm[3], p_norm[4]])


    x := Int.(xy .> 2)
    y := Int.((xy .== 2) .| (xy .== 4))
    p_y = [p_x0[1], p_x1[1]][x .+ 1]

    y_rep = Array{Int}(undef, N)
    loglik = [logpdf(Bernoulli(p_y[i]), y[i]) for i in 1:N]
    for i in 1:N
        if xy[i] < 3
            y_rep[i] = rand(Bernoulli(p_x0[1]))
        else
            y_rep[i] = rand(Bernoulli(p_x1[1]))
        end
    end

    mu1 := mu[1]
    mu2 := mu[2]
    return (mu1=mu1, mu2=mu2, rho=rho, y_rep=y_rep, loglik=loglik)
end


```

```{julia}

function get_vcv(tree; taxa=taxa)
    root = getroot(tree)
    tips = getleaves(tree)
    tip_names = getleafnames(tree)
    vcv = zeros(length(tips), length(tips))

    # Compute VCV matrix (upper triangle only)
    for i in 1:length(tips)
        for j in i:length(tips)
            if i == j
                # Diagonal: total distance from root to tip (variance)
                vcv[i, j] = distance(tree, root, tips[i])
            else
                # Off-diagonal: shared evolutionary time (distance from root to MRCA)
                vcv[j, i] = vcv[i, j] = distance(tree, root, mrca(tree, [tips[i], tips[j]]))
            end
        end
    end
    return vcv[indexin(tip_names, taxa), indexin(tip_names, taxa)]
end

```

```{julia}

vcv_matrices = [get_vcv(t, taxa=taxa) for t in pruned_trees]

```



```{julia}

n_data = length(d.x)
n_trees = length(vcv_matrices)
α = rand(LocationScale(0, 2.5, TDist(3)))
β = rand(Normal(0, 2))
u_rate = rand(Normal(0, 1))
rate = exp(u_rate)
vcv = rand(vcv_matrices)
η = α .+ β .* d.x


a = log.(d.y)
b = -log.(1 .- d.y)
ll = log(mvnormcdf(η, rate * vcv, a, b)[1])

```


```{julia}
@model function brownian_regression(vcv_matrices, x, y)
    n_data = length(x)
    n_trees = length(vcv_matrices)

    # Priors
    α ~ LocationScale(0, 2.5, TDist(3))
    β ~ Normal(0, 2)
    u_rate ~ Normal(0, 1)
    rate := exp(u_rate)
    # latent_index ~ Normal(0, 1)
    # tree_index := clamp(Int(ceil(cdf(Normal(0.0, 1.0), latent_index) * n_trees)), 1, n_trees)
    tree_index ~ Categorical(ones(n_trees) ./ n_trees)

    vcv = vcv_matrices[tree_index]
    a = map(yi -> yi == 1 ? 0.0 : -Inf, y)
    b = map(yi -> yi == 1 ? Inf : 0.0, y)

    ll = log(mvnormcdf(α .+ β .* x, rate * vcv, a, b)[1])
    Turing.@addlogprob! ll
end


```


```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}

model_brownian_regression = brownian_regression(vcv_matrices, d.x, d.y)
chain_brownian_regression = sample(
    model_brownian_regression,
    Gibbs(
        :tree_index => MH(),
        (:α, :β, :rate) => NUTS()
    ),
    20,
    progress=true,
)

# Print summary of the chain
display(chain_brownian_regression[:, [:α, :β, :rate, :tree_index], :])


plot(chain_brownian_regression[:, [:α, :β, :rate, :tree_index], :])

```
